concept.technique_name: sinusoidal waveform period and phase shift

examples.problem_statement: If a waveform has a frequency of $200$ kHz, determine the periodic time.

solution.description: Read the frequency out of the problem and restate it in hertz: 200 kHz means 200 thousand cycles per second, or 200 times 10 to the third hertz. Converting first keeps the later arithmetic in SI units.

solution.operation: Recall the relationship between periodic time and frequency
solution.description: The periodic time is how long one complete cycle takes, and it is the reciprocal of the frequency, so write T equals 1 over f before any numbers go in.

solution.operation: Substitute the given frequency into the formula
solution.description: Substitute the converted frequency, 200 times 10 to the third hertz, into T equals 1 over f.
Carry out the division: 1 divided by 200000 is 0.000005 second, written more compactly as 5 times 10 to the minus 6 seconds.
Since one microsecond is 10 to the minus 6 seconds, the same period reads as 5 microseconds, which is the natural unit for a period this short.
Check by reversing the step: 1 divided by 5 microseconds returns 200000 Hz, which is the 200 kHz originally given, so the period is right.

examples.problem_statement: Sketch y = 7 sin(2A - π/3) in the range 0 ≤ A ≤ 360°

solution.description: Read the amplitude and period straight off the equation. The coefficient 7 sets the peak height at 7, and the coefficient 2 on A compresses the wave, so one full cycle takes 180 degrees instead of 360.

solution.operation: Determine phase shift using general form.
solution.description: Compare with the general form y = A sin(pA minus alpha). The phase shift is alpha divided by p, so divide pi over 3 by 2 to get pi over 6; because the angle is subtracted, the wave lags and shifts to the right.
Draw the curve using those three numbers: peak 7, one cycle every 180 degrees, and the cycle starting at the shifted position rather than at the origin, repeating until A reaches 360 degrees.

examples.problem_statement: Sketch y = 2 cos(ωt - 3π/10) over one cycle

solution.description: Take the amplitude from the coefficient in front of the cosine, so the curve swings between plus and minus 2, and take the period from the angular velocity, since one cycle covers 2 pi over omega in time.
The angle subtracted inside the bracket, 3 pi over 10, lags the wave. Dividing it by omega converts that angle into a shift in time, so the cosine reaches its maximum later than a plain cosine would.
Sketch a single cycle from the amplitude, period and rightward shift just found, starting the drawing at the displaced maximum rather than at t equals zero.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember that adding a positive angle inside the sine or cosine function results in a phase lead (left shift), while subtracting results in a phase lag (right shift).'}
{'point': 'Note: The phase shift for a function y = sin(pt - α) is α/p.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Always check whether the phase shift is expressed in degrees or radians and convert if necessary.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: Memorize common phase shifts like 30° = π/6 rad to quickly identify and sketch waveforms.'}
common_mistakes: Forgetting to divide the phase angle by the coefficient of A: in y = 7 sin(2A - pi/3) the shift is pi/6, not pi/3.
Treating a subtracted angle as a shift to the left; a minus sign inside the bracket lags the wave to the right.
Leaving the period at 360 degrees when the coefficient 2 on A has halved it to 180 degrees.

concept.technique_name: sinusoidal general form A sin(wt + a)

examples.problem_statement: An alternating current is given by i = 30 sin(100πt + 0.35) amperes. Find the (a) amplitude, (b) frequency, (c) periodic time and (d) phase angle (in degrees and minutes)

solution.description: Line the given current up against the general sinusoid i = A sin(wt + phi). The number multiplying the sine is the amplitude, so reading 30 off i = 30 sin(100 pi t + 0.35) gives a peak current of 30 amperes.
The angular frequency is whatever multiplies t inside the bracket, which here is 100 pi radians per second.
Angular frequency and ordinary frequency are tied together by omega equals 2 pi f, so divide the angular frequency by 2 pi; the pi cancels and leaves 50 hertz.
Once the frequency is known the periodic time follows immediately as its reciprocal: 1 divided by 50 gives 0.02 second for one cycle.
The 0.35 sitting inside the bracket is an angle in radians. Multiply by 180 over pi to read it in degrees, which gives about 20.05 degrees.

solution.operation: Convert decimal degrees to degrees and minutes
solution.description: The question asks for degrees and minutes, so split off the decimal part and multiply it by 60: 0.0535 of a degree is about 3 minutes, making the phase angle 20 degrees 3 minutes.

examples.problem_statement: An oscillating mechanism has a maximum displacement of 2.5 m and a frequency of 60 Hz. At time t = 0 the displacement is 90 cm. Express the displacement in the general form A sin(ωt ± α)

solution.description: The maximum displacement is exactly what amplitude means, so A is 2.5 metres, the coefficient that will sit in front of the sine.
Turn the given 60 Hz into the angular velocity the general form needs, using omega equals 2 pi f, which gives 120 pi radians per second as the coefficient of t.
Assemble the two values into the requested shape, displacement equals 2.5 sin(120 pi t plus alpha) metres, leaving the phase angle alpha as the only unknown.

Pin alpha down with the stated condition that the displacement is 90 cm, that is 0.90 m, at t equals 0. Setting t to zero makes the bracket equal alpha, so 2.5 sin alpha equals 0.90 determines the phase shift.

examples.answer: displacement = 2.5 sin(120πt + α) m (calculation of α continues on next page)

Also, (f) sketch one cycle of the waveform

solution.result: v = A\sin(\omega t + \phi) \text{ where } A \text{ is amplitude, } \omega \text{ is angular frequency, } \phi \text{ is phase angle}
solution.description: The general form of a sinusoidal voltage is compared to the given equation to extract parameters.

solution.operation: Calculate amplitude, frequency, periodic time, and phase angle
solution.result: A = 340\text{ V}, \omega = 50\pi\text{ rad/s}, f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = 25\text{ Hz}, T = \frac{1}{f} = 0.04\text{ s}, \phi = -0.541\text{ rad} = -31^\circ
solution.description: Amplitude is the coefficient of sine. Angular frequency is the coefficient of t. Frequency is ω/2π. Periodic time is 1/f. Phase angle is converted from radians to degrees.
With t set to zero the bracket collapses to the phase angle alone, so the voltage is 340 times the sine of minus 0.541 radians, about minus 175.1 volts; the wave starts below zero because it lags.

solution.operation: Find voltage at t = 10 ms = 0.01 s
solution.description: Convert 10 ms into 0.01 s before substituting. The bracket becomes 50 pi times 0.01 minus 0.541, that is 1.5708 minus 0.541, and 340 times the sine of 1.0298 radians gives about 291.4 volts.

solution.operation: Find time when voltage first reaches 200 V
solution.description: To find when the voltage first reaches 200 V, set the expression equal to 200 and divide by 340 so the sine of the bracket is 0.5882. Take the inverse sine to get 0.6289 radians, add the 0.541 phase back on, then divide by 50 pi, giving about 7.45 ms.

solution.operation: Find time when voltage is maximum (340 V)
solution.description: The voltage is largest when the sine equals 1, which happens when the bracket equals pi over 2. Add the 0.541 phase and divide by 50 pi to place that peak at about 13.44 ms.

Draw one cycle using the numbers already found: it starts at about minus 175.1 V at t equals 0, rises through zero at roughly 3.4 ms, peaks at 340 V at 13.44 ms, swings down to minus 340 V half a period later, and closes the 40 ms cycle.

examples.problem_statement: In a school there are 180 students of which 72 are girls. Express this as a fraction in its simplest form

solution.description: Pull out the two numbers the question turns on: 180 students in the school and 72 of them girls.
A fraction compares a part with the whole, so place the 72 girls over the 180 students to get 72 over 180.

solution.operation: Find GCD of numerator and denominator
solution.description: Simplest form means top and bottom share no factor, so find the greatest common divisor of 72 and 180, which is 36.

solution.operation: Divide numerator and denominator by GCD
solution.description: Divide both numerator and denominator by that 36: 72 divided by 36 is 2 and 180 divided by 36 is 5, leaving two fifths.

solution.operation: Verify the fraction is in simplest form
solution.description: Confirm nothing is left to cancel. The greatest common divisor of 2 and 5 is 1, so two fifths really is the simplest form.

examples.problem_statement: Simplify $\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2}$

solution.operation: Find LCM of denominators 3 and 2: LCM = 6
solution.description: Fractions can only be added once they are measured in the same sized pieces, so take the lowest common multiple of the denominators 3 and 2, which is 6.
Rescale the first fraction into sixths by multiplying top and bottom by 2, turning one third into two sixths without changing its value.
Rescale the second fraction the same way, multiplying top and bottom by 3, so one half becomes three sixths.
Both parts are now counted in sixths, so add the numerators 2 and 3 and keep the denominator, giving five sixths.

examples.problem_statement: Simplify $\frac{3}{4} - \frac{7}{16}$

solution.operation: Find LCM of denominators 4 and 16: LCM = 16
solution.description: Check the denominators before doing any work: 16 is already a multiple of 4, so the lowest common multiple of 4 and 16 is just 16.
Multiply the top and bottom of three quarters by 4 to rewrite it in sixteenths as twelve sixteenths.
The second fraction is already expressed in sixteenths, so it is carried straight down with nothing changed.
With a shared denominator, subtract the numerators only: 12 minus 7 is 5, so the answer is five sixteenths.

solution.description: Note the starting point: x is 3 and y is 4, the horizontal and vertical distances that must be traded for a distance and a direction.

concept.technique_name: Cartesian to polar conversion with quadrant adjustment

examples.problem_statement: Express in polar co-ordinates the position (−4, 3)

solution.description: The polar radius is the distance from the origin, the square root of x squared plus y squared. Squaring wipes out the minus sign on the 4, so 16 plus 9 gives 25 and r is 5; a radius is never negative.

solution.operation: Identify the quadrant of the point
solution.description: Before touching the angle, place the point: x is negative while y is positive, so it lies in the second quadrant. This matters because the inverse tangent on its own only ever reports an angle in the first or fourth quadrant.
Find the acute angle the line makes with the x axis by taking the inverse tangent of 3 over 4 using sizes only and ignoring the signs, which gives a reference angle of about 36.87 degrees.

solution.operation: Determine the polar angle θ in degrees
solution.description: Turn that reference angle into the true polar angle. Measured counterclockwise from the positive x axis, a second quadrant direction is 180 degrees minus the reference angle, giving about 143.13 degrees.
If radian measure is wanted, multiply the degree value by pi over 180, so 143.13 degrees becomes about 2.498 radians.
State the result as an ordered pair of radius then angle: 5 at about 143.13 degrees, or the same point as 5 at about 2.498 radians.

solution.description: Find the radius from the two coordinates, squaring 5 and 12 so their signs drop out; 25 plus 144 is 169, whose square root is 13.
Take the inverse tangent of 12 over 5, using the sizes without signs, to get a reference angle of about 67.38 degrees.

Both coordinates are negative, so the point is in the third quadrant. Measuring counterclockwise, add the reference angle to 180 degrees for about 247.38 degrees, or pi plus 1.176 which is about 4.318 radians.

solution.operation: State final polar coordinates: (13, 247.38°) or (13, 4.318 rad)
